Stage 2d: the regional core with China

Stage 2c’s equations on a re-partitioned world — six entities, a euro-area bloc, and the first economy this project had to assemble from scratch

What this stage is

Stage 2d changes who the model is about, and nothing else. Every equation is the one stage 2c settled on — the speed-limit Phillips curve, foreign demand over partner imports, the sovereign spread in place of the long-rate level, and the intertemporal-substitution term in consumption. What changes is the partition of the world:

stage 2c stage 2d
entities 11 countries de, fr, it, us, cn, reu
estimation window 2000Q1–2024Q4 (T = 98) 2005Q1–2024Q4 (T = 78)
stochastic equations 68 38
identities 46 25
policy rules ea_policy_rate, us_policy_rate those plus cn_policy_rate
k 76 46
df 22 32

Two of the six entities are not ordinary countries.

  • reu is a bloc: the seven modelled euro-area economies other than Germany, France and Italy, aggregated into one pseudo-country with its own equations, its own row and column in the trade-weight matrix, and its own foreign_demand identity. Its members contribute no equations of their own.
  • cn is China, the first economy this project has had to assemble rather than fetch. It is also the only one whose block departs from the stage-2c template, and it departs for a data reason, not a modelling preference.

The headline is the degrees of freedom. Every earlier structural change in this project bought detail at the cost of df — stage 3a went from 22 to 15 to 6, stage 3b to 8. Stage 2d runs the other way: collapsing seven countries into one bloc removes enough equations that k falls from 76 to 46, and even after giving up eighteen quarters at the start of the sample df rises from 22 to 32. This is the most comfortably identified joint system the project has estimated.

The two constructed entities

reu: the rest of the euro area

Nominal-GDP weights within the reu bloc (bloc_gdp_weights()).
member weight
AT 0.0996
BE 0.1239
ES 0.3312
GR 0.0481
IE 0.1091
NL 0.2282
PT 0.0599

Every reu_<concept> series is built from those weights, with the aggregator chosen by the series’ own attributes: a level concept (every volume, every price index) is chained in growth space by chain_weighted_index(), and a rate concept (unemployment, long_rate) is a weighted average of levels. The distinction is the one that governs ea_gdp and <iso2>_foreign_demand already — log(sum_i w_i x_i) != sum_i w_i log(x_i), and koma differences everything before it estimates.

The bloc’s identity weights are its members’ shares averaged, and getting that wrong is easy. expenditure_shares() forms each share as the mean of a level ratio, which works for a real country because its series share a currency and a scale. Every bloc series is a base-100 chain index instead, so the ratio is not a share at all — it is the two indices’ relative growth since the base period. Measured on this panel, mean(reu_exports / reu_gdp) comes out at 1.337: reu exports grew 2.5x since 2000 while its GDP grew 1.6x, and the ratio reports that rather than an export share. koma has no identity-consistency check, so the wrong weight would have been enforced in silence. bloc_expenditure_shares() averages the members’ own shares instead:

reu_gdp identity weights, from the members’ shares. Note reu_exports at 0.598, not 1.337 – Ireland and the Netherlands carry very large trade shares, so the bloc is more open than the euro area as a whole.
component weight
reu_domestic_demand 0.941
reu_exports 0.598
reu_imports -0.548

The name is rest of the euro area, not rest of the EU. The bloc covers the seven modelled EA economies, which is what the panel has data for; it is not the EU, and it is not the whole euro area either (the six smallest members were never in modelled_countries). Everything genuinely outside the six stage-2d entities still goes to row_gdp, so nothing is double-counted — but reu_gdp is not a published aggregate and should not be compared against one.

cn: China, and the one thing the public data does not have

China publishes no quarterly expenditure-side national accounts, and that is a fact about the data rather than a gap in the search. Verified absent from:

  • OECD Quarterly National Accounts — carries B1GQ for China and nothing else, and only from 2011Q1;
  • OECD Economic Outlook — annual for everything except CPI and two interest rates, and even annually it has no CPV/IGV for China;
  • IMF International Financial Statistics — real GDP from 2011Q1, no expenditure split;
  • World Bank GEM, FRED (China coverage discontinued between 2019 and
    1. and the NBS itself.

So cn_consumption and cn_investment do not exist. The alternative to inventing them from indicator proxies — retail sales, fixed-asset investment — is to merge them, and that is what merged_demand_countries does:

cn_domestic_demand ~ cn_gdp + cn_long_rate + cn_domestic_demand.L(1)
cn_exports         ~ cn_foreign_demand + cn_exports.L(1)
cn_imports         ~ cn_domestic_demand + cn_imports.L(1)
cn_prices          ~ eur_usd + oil_price + cn_gdp + cn_prices.L(1)
cn_spread          ~ cn_prices + cn_gdp + cn_spread.L(1)
cn_policy_rate     ~ cn_prices + cn_gdp + cn_policy_rate.L(1)

cn_gdp            == 0.958*cn_domestic_demand + 0.243*cn_exports - 0.201*cn_imports
cn_long_rate      == 1*cn_spread + 1*cn_policy_rate
cn_foreign_demand == (trade-weighted partner imports)

The rate term survives the merge unconditionally, because it was investment’s term as well as consumption’s and it is China’s only monetary channel. What is given up is the split: there is no separate MPC or accelerator to read off. Net cost is one equation and one column of k.

Three constructions, each stated because each is one

Trade volumes are deflated, not taken as published. GEM’s constant-price China trade series are missing every first quarter from 2020Q1 to 2025Q1 — six of the eighty quarters in the window, all in the middle of the sample, where koma cannot estimate across them at all. (China’s customs administration stopped publishing a separate January figure, merging January and February to smooth the moving Lunar New Year.) The current-price and price-index series are complete, so the volume is recovered as value / price — the same quotient GEM computes internally, reproducing the published series where both exist to a mean ratio of 0.99985 (sd 4.4e-4) for exports and 0.99974 (sd 9.4e-4) for imports. That recovers six real quarters instead of interpolating them.

Units are reconciled by a constant rescaling. GDP is constant local currency and the trade volumes are constant US dollars; the three cannot be added. Both volume series are rescaled by a single constant so their window mean equals the mean nominal trade share of GDP times mean real GDP, the shares coming from GEM’s own current-dollar series so numerator and denominator share a currency: 0.229 (exports) and 0.188 (imports). A constant multiplicative rescaling changes no growth rate, so koma still differences exactly the published volume index.

Domestic demand is the accounting residual, cn_gdp - cn_exports + cn_imports, which makes the GDP identity exact in level space (verified to 3.7e-9). Because the trade series are merchandise only, the residual absorbs the services balance — for China a persistent services deficit — so cn_domestic_demand is a little larger than true domestic demand and grows a little differently. Same class of approximation as <iso2>_gdp’s statistical discrepancy, and identity_consistency() treats it the same way: reported, never flagged.

The long rate is the weakest series here

The cn_long_rate splice, measured.
quantity value
mean IRLT - IR3TIB -0.262 pp
sd of that gap 0.487 pp
overlapping quarters 50
IRLT begins 2014Q1
quarters spliced in the window 36 of 80

OECD publishes a genuine Chinese 10-year government bond rate, IRLT, but only from 2014Q1 — none of the first 36 quarters of the estimation window. Before that, cn_long_rate is the three-month interbank rate shifted by the mean gap over the overlap. The shift is additive rather than multiplicative because these are rates in percentage points that pass through koma untransformed, and a ratio splice on a series that can approach zero is not safe.

The standard deviation of that gap is nearly twice its mean, so the spliced segment reproduces the level of a Chinese long rate but not its independent variation: before 2014 cn_long_rate moves exactly like the three-month interbank rate. The consequence is specific — cn_spread is a genuine term premium over the second half of the sample and a money-market term spread plus a constant over the first. If that is not acceptable for a given exercise, the clean alternative is stage2d_config(spread_countries = setdiff(stage2d_countries(), "cn")), which lets cn_domestic_demand load cn_policy_rate directly: IRSTCI is complete over the whole window and needs no splice at all.

One further interpolated observation: IR3TIB is missing 2006Q1, which fill_internal_gaps() fills with a warning naming it.

Trade weights, and a wart that had to be fixed

How each row was built.
reporter source
de direct

The euro-area rows come from ECB WTS as everywhere else in this project. The reu row is its members’ rows averaged with GDP weights and intra-bloc trade renormalised away — 16.8% of the averaged row, which has no external counterparty once the seven members are one entity.

The us and cn rows are the fix. ECB WTS computes weights for euro-area reporters only, so stages 1–3 build the US row from the reciprocal of each euro-area country’s own weight on the US, renormalised. Renormalising is where it goes wrong: it forces the modelled partners to account for the reporter’s entire trade. The stage-2b matrix on disk gives the United States a rest-of-world weight of 4.6% and Ireland a 24.7% share of US trade — both plainly false, and both already recorded in CLAUDE.md as known-unreliable. With only six entities, and China now among them, applying the same construction would have given China a rest-of-world weight of 1.0% and put 56% of Chinese trade inside the euro area.

Both rows therefore come from observed IMF Direction of Trade Statistics instead (imf_dots_weights()), where the world total is published and the residual is real: the US at 72.9% rest-of-world and China at 78.2%, with the US–China pair at 11.7% / 11.5%. Two differences from WTS are worth keeping in view, since the two statistics now coexist in one matrix: DOTS is goods only where WTS covers manufactured products and services, and DOTS is a plain trade share where WTS is a double-weighted effective-exchange-rate weight that also accounts for third-market competition.

reu_gdp‘s worst error, at 5.0 percentage points of quarterly growth, is the largest in the table and it should be: on top of the statistical discrepancy a single country carries (Germany 2.0, Italy 1.9), the bloc adds a dispersion term, because its seven members’ own expenditure shares differ from the average the identity uses. It is the price of the aggregation, it is bounded, and it is of the same order as the country-level slack rather than a different animal.

Estimation

tune_tau_system(): flagged equations and the worst acceptance rate per round.

0 6 0.6165

All 38 of 38 equations have a Metropolis step — every one of them has a contemporaneous endogenous regressor, which stage 2c’s Phillips curve is what made true. After tuning, acceptance rates run 39.4%–60.4% against the 20–60% band, with 1 equation (reu_exports) marginally over at 60.4%. The doubling rule oscillates around the boundary rather than converging on it; three rounds took the count from 6 to 1 and a fourth would not help. 17 equations carry a tau override, all at 2.2.

Does the structure work?

Every policy rate reaches every price

contemporaneous_reachability() from each of the three policy rates.
policy rate endogenous reached price variables reached
ea_policy_rate 63 / 63 7
us_policy_rate 63 / 63 7
cn_policy_rate 63 / 63 7

This is the structural claim stage 2c existed to establish, and it survives the re-partition intact. In stage 2b ea_policy_rate reached 91 of 103 endogenous variables and not one price, so the Taylor rule’s inflation term responded to something nothing it did could influence. Here all three policy rates reach all 63 endogenous variables and all seven price variables. Adding a third rule does not weaken it: China’s rule closes its own loop through cn_prices -> cn_policy_rate -> cn_long_rate -> cn_domestic_demand -> cn_gdp -> cn_prices, and reaches the euro area and the US through the trade identities.

Reachability is exact and verifiable. It is not a claim that the response has the right sign or size — stage 2c’s own lesson was that closing the loop structurally did not make the monetary shock work, and only the seed placebo showed it. A spillover battery on this system is the obvious next step and is not in this report.

26 of 30 pass. The two Phillips-curve failures are small and both straddle zero — Italy’s at -0.00294 is indistinguishable from nothing at all. spread_loads_on_prices_positive was already flagged in stage 2c as the weakest of the four a priori, since a flight-to-quality episode compresses spreads while inflation rises. None of the four is in a China or reu equation, which is the useful negative result: the two constructed entities are not where the specification strains.

The merged China equation, judged against the right benchmark

Domestic-demand elasticity to GDP: implied from the split for the five entities that have it, estimated directly for China.
iso2 consumption investment elasticity
de 0.159 1.922 0.633
fr 0.960 0.954 0.959
it 0.725 1.761 0.984
us 0.612 3.869 1.264
reu 0.673 -0.170 0.428
cn NA NA 1.101

The first bound put on this rule was wrong, and the data said so. The obvious rule for a merged demand equation is the MPC’s — a coefficient in (0, 1) — and China’s 1.101 fails it. But an MPC below one is a claim about consumption; total domestic absorption also contains investment, which is far more cyclical than output. Computing the implied elasticity for the five entities that do have the split gives 0.43–1.26, with the United States at 1.264 — so a (0, 1) bound would have reported the US as a failure too. The rule is > 0, and China’s estimate sits inside the range the other five span. Reporting a correct coefficient as a failure because of a rule invented alongside it is exactly the trap this project has hit before.

The rate term in that equation is -0.0188 with a 90% interval of [-0.412, 0.272] — correctly signed and firmly indistinguishable from zero. Given that 36 of the 80 quarters of cn_long_rate are spliced, that is the expected result rather than a surprise, and it is the strongest argument for trying the spread_countries-without-China variant.

What the bloc costs: reu_investment

The investment equations. reu is the most volatile series and the worst-fitting equation, despite being an average of seven economies.
entity sd of growth accelerator (on gdp) in-sample RMSE
de 2.16 1.922 1.22
fr 2.74 0.954 0.78
it 4.08 1.761 1.49
us 3.98 3.869 1.91
reu 6.46 -0.170 4.34

Averaging seven economies should reduce volatility. Here it raises it, and that is the tell. reu_investment has a quarterly growth standard deviation of 6.46, against 2.16–4.08 for the four real countries. The cause is the one this project has already documented for Ireland: ie_investment has a growth sd of 43.0 on this window, against 2.2 for Austria and 3.0 for Portugal, and Ireland carries a 10.9% weight in the bloc — so Ireland alone contributes more to reu_investment’s variance than every other member combined. The Netherlands (sd 14.0) adds most of the rest.

The consequence is that this one equation is not identified. Its accelerator is -0.17 with a 90% interval of [-2.77, 2.14] — wrong-signed, but so wide that the sign carries no information — and its own lag has gone to -0.567, i.e. the equation has collapsed into mean-reversion around noise rather than an accelerator. Its in-sample RMSE is 4.34 against 0.78–1.91 for the others.

There is deliberately no sign rule for the investment accelerator in base_sign_rules(), so nothing flagged this — it surfaced only from computing the implied demand elasticity above, which came out lowest for reu at 0.428. That is the familiar lesson in a new place: a neighbouring coefficient moving is the first symptom, and the check that would have caught it directly does not exist.

Stages 2b and 2c work around Irish measured GDP with ireland_proxy, which swaps the foreign-demand basis for a better-behaved Irish series. That switch is unavailable here, because the distortion is now inside an estimated equation rather than in an identity’s components. Two things would actually help, neither of them attempted in this report: weighting the bloc by something less Ireland-heavy than nominal GDP, or excluding Ireland from reu entirely and carrying it as its own entity or in row_gdp. Until then, read reu_investment as unidentified, and treat reu_domestic_demand — which inherits it through the identity — as correspondingly soft.

What this stage is and is not for

Use it for anything where the euro area’s three largest economies, the US and China need to interact inside one estimated system, and where df = 32 matters more than country detail: cross-bloc spillovers, a China demand or policy shock, the transmission of a US rate move into euro-area activity.

Do not use it for a statement about Austria, Spain, Ireland or any other reu member — they have no equations here, only a weight. Stage 2b or 2c is where those live. And do not compare its coefficients directly against stage 2c’s: the sample is eighteen quarters shorter, and four of the six entities are different objects.

The three things to watch are stated above rather than buried: cn_long_rate is spliced over 45% of the window, reu_investment is not identified because Ireland dominates the bloc’s investment variance, and reu’s identities carry a dispersion term on top of the usual statistical discrepancy. Neither is hidden from the diagnostics — the splice is measured in cn_long_rate_series() and the dispersion shows up in identity_consistency() as the largest error in the table.

Eight-quarter forecast

8 quarters from 2025Q1 to 2026Q4, 1000 posterior draws. Actuals exist for the first 5 quarters; the rest is genuinely ahead of the data.

Every fan below is the filtered predictive interval: koma constrains no draw to be stationary, so a draw whose quarterly growth exceeds 100% in absolute value is dropped before the quantiles are taken, exactly as score_forecast() does when it scores a backtest. The solid band is the 25th-75th percentile of what survives, the faint band the 10th-90th, the dark line their median, and the grey line the realised path where one exists. Across the variables shown, 1.6% of draws are discarded as explosive at horizon 1, rising to 34.1% at horizon 8 (worst: it_gdp at 43.6%). A variable whose discarded share climbs steeply is one whose fan understates the model’s true uncertainty, so read the tail of a wide fan as an ordering rather than a number.

The panels are clipped, and that is worth saying plainly. Eight quarters out, the 10-90 interval on quarterly growth spans tens of percentage points in every stage of this project – an honest number, and one that makes the median invisible if the axis is scaled to contain it. Each panel is therefore scaled to its inner band, and the outer band runs to the panel edge rather than being drawn in full. Nothing is concealed: the table at the end of this section reports the untruncated bounds.

Every level path is anchored on an observed value (largest anchor discrepancy 0.00%, on fr_imports), so the level and rate charts are both directly comparable to the actuals.

A forecast this long needs the exogenous series to reach the end of the horizon, and they do not: every one of them stops at the fit’s own native forecast end. extend_forecast_horizon() carries each one forward on its trailing four-quarter average growth – a momentum continuation, not a view on oil markets or world trade – and koma would otherwise have silently returned a shorter horizon than the one requested.
